title: Hollywood investigated who really directed Poltergeist, and the debate is still alive 44 years later
excerpt: Poltergeist credits Tobe Hooper as director and Steven Spielberg as writer and producer, yet their roles prompted a Directors Guild of America inquiry in 1982. The dispute resurfaced in 2026, inviting another look at what the evidence does, and does not, establish.
content:
Poltergeist credits Tobe Hooper as director and Steven Spielberg as writer and producer, yet their roles prompted a Directors Guild of America inquiry in 1982. The dispute resurfaced in 2026, inviting another look at what the evidence does, and does not, establish.

On the Poltergeist set, Steven Spielberg recalled, he would offer a suggestion when a question went unanswered, and Tobe Hooper would nod in agreement. “He’s just not a strong presence on a movie set,” Spielberg said of Hooper in a 1982 Los Angeles Times interview. It was a pointed account of their collaboration, but not proof of who was directing.

The latest debate began with a collaboration, not a secret plan

The question returned after a May 26, 2026 revival of the directing rumor. Slate followed with its own examination in June. The renewed attention points back to a partnership that began when Spielberg approached Hooper about working together.

Spielberg had a science-fiction idea called Night Skies, but Hooper proposed a ghost story instead. Their arrangement put Hooper in the director’s chair while Spielberg wrote and produced. Spielberg’s contract with Universal for E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial barred him from directing another film while making it, a restriction that has long fed speculation about what happened on the other set.

Spielberg’s comments brought the directors guild into the dispute

Spielberg’s account of their working relationship had consequences beyond the interview. The pre-release Los Angeles Times feature prompted the Directors Guild of America to investigate whether he had effectively directed the film. His description of the collaboration brought official scrutiny to Hooper’s credit.

Guild executive Michael Franklin was direct. “There is a director of ‘Poltergeist’ and he is listed as Tobe Hooper,” he said, adding that guild rules barred a producer from replacing an assigned director. The inquiry’s outcome is less clear. One account reports a $15,000 payment from MGM to Hooper because promotional material downplayed his credit; another describes the investigation as going nowhere. Neither version turns Spielberg’s presence into an established director credit.

People who worked on the film still tell different stories

Later witnesses have kept the dispute alive. Camera crew member John R. Leonetti has said in interviews that Spielberg directed the film. In 2019, filmmaker Scott Derrickson said that he asked star Craig T. Nelson about the rumor, and Nelson maintained that Hooper directed it. Those recollections cannot be made to agree simply by choosing the more confident speaker.

Other stars have likewise denied that Spielberg directed the movie while acknowledging that he was active on set. Accounts of the production describe him as frequently present and exercising significant creative control. Those details make his influence impossible to dismiss, even as the firsthand accounts resist a tidy answer about who directed.

Spielberg defended Hooper’s credit, but the question endured

Spielberg responded publicly after the controversy took hold. In an open letter to Hooper, reported as appearing in The Hollywood Reporter, he said the press had misunderstood their creative relationship and praised Hooper’s direction. He separately wrote to Time for its June 21, 1982 edition, calling an earlier quotation unfair to Hooper and denying that he had taken over the project.

Spielberg’s remarks helped bring guild attention to Hooper’s role, yet Spielberg also defended that role in print. Our take is that Hooper’s director credit deserves defending; accounts that he delivered his cut on October 17, 1981, also point to a question about the scope of his post-production role.
